Newly hatched neonates of Diaphanosoma excisum emerge from the brood chamber at a remarkably small size, with a total length of just 0.057 cm [Lb = 0.057 cm] at birth. This minute body dimension is typical of freshwater cladocerans and reflects the limited maternal investment in each individual offspring. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], these neonates begin filter-feeding almost immediately, initiating a phase of rapid somatic growth. The comparatively short interval between hatching and the onset of reproductive competence is a defining feature of the life history of this species. The time elapsed since birth at the moment when puberty is attained has been measured at 2.25 days [tp = 2.25 days] under these same thermal conditions, a developmental pace that is consistent with the high metabolic rates characteristic of warm-adapted cladoceran zooplankton.

When individuals of Diaphanosoma excisum are reared at 29 °C [T = 29 °C], the age at birth itself is essentially instantaneous following egg release, with the free-swimming neonate stage beginning approximately 1.0 day [ab = approximately 1.0 day] after oviposition. This rapid embryonic development allows for an exceptionally high population turnover rate in ephemeral water bodies. The total length measured at the point of sexual maturation, known as the length at puberty, reaches 0.085 cm [Lp = 0.085 cm]. This transition from juvenile to reproductively active adult is marked by the first appearance of developed ovaries, after which the females quickly begin to produce clutches. The attainment of this pubertal length within just over two days post-birth, as noted under the 29 °C regime, underscores the species’ capacity for rapid colonization of newly formed aquatic habitats, outpacing many co-occurring competitors.

As Diaphanosoma excisum continues its growth trajectory, the ultimate total length it achieves under favorable conditions is 0.134 cm [Li = 0.134 cm]. This asymptotic body size represents the maximum carapace length attained during the adult phase, after which growth plateaus and energetic resources are instead channeled into continuous reproduction. When the dry weight of such fully grown, adult females is measured, it reaches a value of 28.5 micrograms . This low biomass is characteristic of small-bodied cladocerans and has direct implications for their energetic demands, susceptibility to predation by visual planktivores, and overall role in the planktonic food web as grazers of phytoplankton and bacteria.

The reproductive output of Diaphanosoma excisum has been quantified through detailed life-table experiments conducted at 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. An individual female produces approximately 55 neonates over the course of her entire lifetime. The maximum daily reproduction rate, calculated by dividing this lifetime fecundity by the length of the reproductive period of 23.75 days, yields a value of about 2.3 offspring per day [Ri = about 2.3 offspring per day] at 29 °C. This high per-capita output is typical of a ruderal life-history strategy, allowing for explosive population growth when environmental conditions are favorable. Each reproductive event itself typically consists of dozens of parthenogenetically produced subitaneous eggs, which develop rapidly within the brood chamber before being released as miniature versions of the adult.

The maximum lifespan of Diaphanosoma excisum when maintained at 29 °C [T = 29 °C] has been recorded at 26 days [am = 26 days] in the laboratory. This relatively brief longevity is characteristic of a small, fast-living zooplankter that invests heavily in early reproduction at the expense of extended somatic maintenance. The end of life typically occurs after a period of declining fecundity, as the metabolic costs of continued reproduction eventually become unsustainable. In natural pond environments, this theoretical maximum is seldom realized due to intense predation pressure from insects and small fish, although dormant resting eggs allow the population to persist across unfavorable seasons. The species thus exemplifies a classic trade-off between rapid development, high early fecundity, and a short adult lifespan.
